The Inuit. The indigenous circumpolar peoples of the Arctic who inhabit some of Earth's most extreme environments and developed sophisticated maritime hunting cultures adapted to these harsh conditions. The Inuit inhabit the Arctic regions across Alaska, Northern Canada, Greenland, and eastern Russia. Their territories span one of the most extreme environments on the planet. They speak Inuit-Yupik languages, part of the Eskimo-Aleut language family, with multiple distinct languages and dialects. Inuktitut, Inupiatun, and Kalaallisut, also known as Greenlandic, are major varieties. The Inuit developed sophisticated marine hunting traditions targeting seals, whales, and fish using specialized equipment including kayaks, originally called qajaq, along with harpoons and nets. Dog sledding, teams of dogs used for winter transportation across frozen landscapes, was historically central to mobility and trade and remains culturally significant in some communities today. The Inuit created intricate art forms including tupilak carvings, which are spiritual figures, along with ivory carving and drum-making. Oral traditions preserved narratives and ecological knowledge passed down through generations. Historically, the Inuit lived in seasonal camps and settlements adapted to animal migrations and seasonal changes, developing efficient housing including igloo snow houses in certain regions. Today, the Inuit number approximately one hundred and eighty thousand across the Arctic. They face ongoing challenges from climate change, cultural preservation, and self-determination, and increasingly advocate for indigenous rights and environmental protection.
